disclaimer.title: What this site is — and is not
disclaimer.full: Kasian Sultan is a free educational project. It is not investment, tax, or legal advice, and no part of it is a recommendation to buy or sell any fund, security, or product. It is not operated by a licensed securities professional, financial advisor, or tax preparer, and is not affiliated with any financial institution or government agency. The calculators are illustrations driven entirely by assumptions you choose; projections are mathematical scenarios, not predictions or guarantees — real markets rise, fall, and misbehave, and past or assumed returns do not determine future results. Tax rules shown are for tax year 2026 (B.E. 2569), verified against the sources listed below on the date shown, and change often — confirm current rules with the Revenue Department (rd.go.th) before acting. Before making investment, tax, or retirement decisions, consult a licensed professional: an SEC-licensed investment advisor for investments, or a qualified tax advisor for your filing. Nothing you enter here is collected, stored, or transmitted — all calculations run and remain in your browser (your language choice is saved on your own device only).

hero.title: Kasian Sultan
hero.sub: A free guide to retiring in Thailand — the maths, the tax, the dates that matter.
hero.privacy: Nothing you type leaves this page

time.title: Time is the asset.
time.lede: Not your salary. Not your stock picks. The years you leave money alone are the part nobody can buy back later.
time.doublings: times money invested today could double by 65 at 6% — the rule of 72, an illustration, not a promise
time.note: The rule of 72: divide 72 by your return to estimate the years each doubling takes. At 6% that is roughly 12 years. It is a mental shortcut, not a forecast — real returns arrive unevenly, and some years are negative.

number.title: Your number.
number.lede: Retirement is not an age. It is a pile of money large enough that what it produces covers what you spend.
number.guaranteedNote: SSO pension, rent you collect, a company pension — income that arrives whether or not your portfolio behaves.
number.target: Portfolio that could fund the rest
number.range: at a {low}–{high} starting withdrawal rate (research as of {date}) — assumptions, not magic
number.multiples: That is {lowX}× to {highX}× your portfolio-funded yearly spending.
number.essNote: Essentials are the floor that must be funded no matter what happens. Discretionary spending is where flexibility lives — people who can cut back in bad years can safely start at a higher rate than people who cannot.

climb.title: The climb.
climb.band: The shaded band is the middle 90% of 1,000 simulated futures — a range, not a promise. All figures are in today's baht, so you can read them with today's prices in mind.
climb.seq: Take ten years of returns averaging exactly 5%, a ฿1,000,000 portfolio, and ฿50,000 withdrawn each year. Nothing changes except the order the returns arrive in:
climb.seqNote: Same returns. Same average. A 46% gap in what you are left with. This is sequence-of-returns risk, and it is why a single average return figure flatters a plan.

rules.title: The rules of the game.
rules.lede: Almost everyone misunderstands this one thing, and it costs them money and sleep.
rules.marginal: marginal rate — tax on your NEXT baht
rules.effective: effective rate — tax across ALL your baht
rules.myth: Crossing into a higher bracket never taxes your whole income at the new rate — only the slice above the line. A raise cannot shrink your take-home pay.
rules.assume: Assumes salaried income with the standard expense deduction and the personal allowance only — no spouse, children, or other deductions. An illustration, not your filing.
rules.demoNote: A made-up three-band country, so you can watch the mechanism without Thai numbers in the way. Every progressive tax system on earth works like this.

cheats.title: The cheat codes.
cheats.lede: The legal ones. Thailand pays you to save for your own retirement — but only up to lines that most people have never seen drawn.
cheats.ceilRet: shared retirement ceiling — RMF + PVD + GPF + NSF + pension insurance
cheats.esgNote: Thai ESG's enhanced ฿300,000 cap ends 31 December 2026 (B.E. 2569) unless it is extended. After that it is expected to revert to a smaller cap with a longer holding period.
cheats.pensionTrap: Pension life insurance counts INSIDE the ฿500,000 retirement ceiling, not alongside it. This is the single most commonly misfiled deduction in Thailand.
cheats.note: A simulator, not a filing. Caps depend on your income, and they change from tax year to tax year. Also inside the shared ceiling but not shown here: GPF and NSF. Confirm everything before you file.

cal.title: The calendar.
cal.lede: Money decisions have deadlines. Miss the December one and a whole year of deductions is simply gone.
cal.filingNote: Paper deadline 31 March 2027. An 8-day e-filing extension has been granted in recent years, but the current authorisation lapses 31 January 2027 — check rd.go.th each season rather than assuming it.
cal.pnd94Note: Only if you have rental, freelance, or other section 40(5)–(8) income earned January to June. Salary alone never triggers it.
cal.cutoffNote: RMF and Thai ESG purchases must settle within 2026 to count for 2026. The exact final dealing day varies by fund — buy by mid-December to be safe.
cal.esgNote: The last day of the ฿300,000 enhanced deduction era, unless it is extended.
cal.taviNote: Your employer must issue the withholding tax certificate by 15 February. You cannot file accurately without it.
cal.minelede: These move with the age you set in chapter one.
cal.rmf55note: From 55, and after holding at least five years, RMF can be redeemed without losing the tax relief.
cal.nsf60note: The National Savings Fund starts paying its pension at 60.
cal.exempt65note: From 65 you can exempt up to ฿190,000 of income before the standard expense deduction.
cal.sso: The SSO pension needs 180 months of contributions — fifteen years. At the 2026 wage ceiling that is about ฿3,500 a month from age 55, rising by 1.5 percentage points for each extra year you contribute. Below 180 months you get a lump sum instead. Check your months at sso.go.th.

instruments.title: The instruments.
instruments.lede: What you can actually buy in Thailand, what each one is for, and how each is taxed. No product names, no suggestions — just what the tools are.
instruments.mixTitle: How allocations usually shift with age
instruments.mix: The textbook pattern is simple: the further you are from needing the money, the more of it tends to sit in growth assets, because you have time to ride out falls. In your twenties that usually means mostly growth assets. Around midlife it typically becomes a genuine mix. Near and into retirement it usually tilts towards stability and income, because a bad year hurts far more when you are selling rather than buying. These are illustrations of a common pattern, not a recommendation for you — your own mix depends on circumstances this page knows nothing about.
instruments.windfallTitle: A lump sum is a different question
instruments.windfall: Research on investing a windfall all at once versus spreading it out generally favours investing promptly — markets rise more often than they fall, so waiting usually costs you. Vanguard found lump-sum investing beat spreading it over three months about 68% of the time. That research is about a windfall: a bonus, an inheritance, a provident fund payout. It says nothing about investing your salary monthly, which is simply how salaries arrive — that is not a suboptimal strategy, it is your cash flow.
instruments.foreign: If you are a Thai tax resident — 180 days or more in the country in a year — foreign income you earned from 2024 onward is taxable when you bring it into Thailand, in that year or any later one. Income earned before 2024 is not caught by this. A relaxation has been drafted but is not law as of August 2026. Foreign gains are taxed as ordinary income at up to 35% when remitted, while gains on Thai listed shares are exempt — a difference big enough to be worth professional advice if it applies to you.

savings.name: Savings account
savings.what: A bank deposit you can withdraw at any time. Not an investment — a place to keep the money you might need this month, and the emergency fund you hope not to touch.
savings.risk: Effectively none, aside from inflation quietly eroding what it buys.
savings.tax: Interest is subject to 15% withholding tax, but savings-account interest up to ฿20,000 a year is exempt.

deposit.name: Fixed deposit
deposit.what: A bank deposit locked for a set term at a set rate. Slightly more interest in exchange for not touching it.
deposit.risk: Very low. The rate is known in advance.
deposit.liq: Locked for the term; breaking it early usually costs you the interest.
deposit.tax: 15% withholding tax on the interest. You may include it in your return instead and claim the tax back if your rate is lower.

sso.name: Social Security (SSO)
sso.what: Not something you buy — if you are employed, you are already contributing. It pays an old-age pension, plus medical and unemployment cover along the way.
sso.risk: None to you; it is a state scheme.
sso.liq: Pension from 55 with at least 180 months of contributions. Fewer months means a lump sum instead.
sso.tax: Your contributions are deductible. Check your contribution months at sso.go.th.

pvd.name: Provident fund (PVD)
pvd.what: A retirement fund run through your employer, who usually contributes alongside you. The employer match is the closest thing to free money in this whole list.
pvd.risk: Depends on the plan you choose inside it, from conservative to growth.
pvd.liq: Tied to your employment and the fund's rules.
pvd.tax: Contributions deductible up to 15% of wages, inside the shared ฿500,000 retirement ceiling.

rmf.name: RMF — retirement mutual fund
rmf.what: A mutual fund wrapper designed for retirement, with tax relief in exchange for genuinely leaving it alone. You choose what it invests in.
rmf.risk: Whatever the underlying fund holds — from money-market to global equity.
rmf.liq: Locked until 55, and at least five years of holding. Breaking the rules means repaying the relief.
rmf.tax: Deductible up to 30% of income, capped at ฿500,000, inside the shared retirement ceiling.

esg.name: Thai ESG fund
esg.what: A fund investing in Thai companies meeting sustainability criteria, created to encourage long-term domestic investment.
esg.risk: Concentrated in the Thai market, so it rises and falls with one country's economy.
esg.tax: Deductible up to 30% of income, capped at ฿300,000 — and this one stacks separately from the ฿500,000 retirement ceiling. The enhanced cap ends 31 December 2026 unless extended.

fund.name: Index and mutual funds
fund.what: A single purchase that spreads your money across many companies at once. The usual starting point for someone who does not want to pick individual shares.
fund.risk: Varies with what it tracks, but far less concentrated than owning a handful of shares.
fund.liq: Generally sell any business day; the money settles in a few days.
fund.tax: Gains on redeeming units are exempt from personal income tax. Distributions are treated differently — check the fund's documents.

stock.name: Thai listed shares (SET)
stock.what: Direct part-ownership of individual companies traded on the Thai exchange.
stock.risk: High and concentrated. One company can fall a long way on its own news.
stock.tax: Capital gains on listed shares sold on the exchange are exempt from personal income tax. Dividends carry 10% withholding tax, with an option to include them in your return and claim a credit.

bond.name: Bonds
bond.what: Lending money to the government or a company for a fixed period at a fixed rate. You are a lender, not an owner.
bond.risk: Lower than shares. Government bonds are the safer end; company bonds pay more because they can default.
bond.liq: Government bonds can usually be sold; some retail bonds are meant to be held to maturity.
bond.tax: Interest is subject to 15% withholding tax, the same as deposit interest.

gold.name: Gold
gold.what: A store of value people turn to when they distrust everything else. It produces no income at all — no interest, no dividends.
gold.risk: Prices swing widely and can go nowhere for years at a stretch.
gold.liq: Physical gold sells readily in Thailand; gold funds trade like funds.
gold.tax: Treatment depends on the form you hold it in — physical, fund, or futures are not the same. Check before you assume.

begin.title: Begin.
begin.lede: You now know more about this than most people ever will. Here is what this site is, where every number came from, and what to do next.
begin.again: Change your assumptions and climb again
begin.privacy2: This page has no accounts, no analytics, no cookies, and no server. Your numbers never left your browser — close the tab and they are gone. Only your language choice is remembered, on your own device.
begin.next: Find out how many SSO contribution months you have. Check whether your employer offers a provident fund and whether you are taking the full match. Work out your marginal rate from chapter four, and only then decide whether a deduction is worth it to you. If any of it is a large decision, take it to a licensed advisor — this site is a map, not a guide who knows your terrain.
